topic: Design case studies: location tracking, media upload & search

questions.question: Ride-hailing driver app: during an active trip the driver switches to a navigation app, and the rider must still see the car move. How should the driver app keep sending location?
options: A foreground service of type `location` with an ongoing trip notification
A periodic WorkManager job that reads the location every 15 minutes
A coroutine launched in the trip screen's `viewModelScope`
An exact alarm that wakes the app every 5 seconds
questions.explanation: Continuous, user-visible tracking is exactly what a location-type foreground service is for, and the notification tells the driver tracking is on. The cost is a permanent notification and more battery use, which is acceptable during a trip. Periodic WorkManager has a 15-minute minimum, a ViewModel scope dies with the screen, and frequent exact alarms are restricted and drain the battery.

questions.question: Delivery driver app: couriers complain that live tracking drains the battery during an 8-hour shift. Which changes cut battery use while keeping tracking useful? Select all that apply.
options: Use `setMaxUpdateDelayMillis` so fixes are batched and delivered together, letting the radio and CPU sleep in between
Lower the priority and interval (e.g. balanced power, 30s) while the courier is idle between orders, and switch to high accuracy only during an active delivery
Skip the upload when the courier hasn't moved more than a small distance since the last sent point
Request `PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY` at 1-second intervals for the whole shift so the fix is always fresh
Open a new HTTPS connection for every single fix so no connection stays open
questions.explanation: The trade-off is freshness and accuracy against battery: batching, state-based priority and distance thresholds give up a little latency where nobody needs it. Constant 1-second high-accuracy GPS is the main drain, and a new TLS connection per fix wakes the radio far more often than one batched upload.

questions.question: Driver app: tracking runs only in a location foreground service that the driver starts from the visible app with a Start trip button. On Android 10+ the app must also hold `ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION` for this to work.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A location-type foreground service started while the app is visible counts as while-in-use access, so foreground location permission (plus the foreground service permissions) is enough. Background location is a separate permission that Play reviews closely, and you only need it when location is read with no visible UI or foreground service, so avoiding it keeps both the permission flow and the policy review simple.

questions.question: Ride-hailing driver app: the car drives through a 2-minute tunnel with no signal. What should happen to the location fixes collected meanwhile?
options: Discard them, since only the newest position matters
Stop requesting location until the network comes back
Buffer timestamped fixes locally and upload them as a batch on reconnect
Keep each failed request retrying in memory until it succeeds, so no point is lost
questions.explanation: The live marker only needs the latest point, but the server also needs the full trail for trip distance, fare and disputes. A bounded, persisted buffer of timestamped points serves both. In-memory retries are lost if the process dies and pile up into many parallel requests, and dropping points breaks fare calculation.

questions.question: Ride-hailing rider app: the driver's position arrives every ~4 seconds and the car icon jumps across the map. What is the best fix?
options: Ask the driver app to send a fix every 200ms so the marker moves smoothly
Animate the marker from its last position and bearing to the new one
Redraw the whole map each time an update arrives
Show the driver's position only when the rider taps a refresh button
questions.explanation: Interpolating on the client makes the movement look smooth at no network or battery cost, in exchange for showing the car slightly behind real time. Sending updates 20x more often would drain the driver's battery and data just to hide a rendering problem.

questions.question: Ride-hailing rider app: how should it receive the driver's live position and trip events? Select all sound choices.
options: Keep a WebSocket (or similar stream) open while the trip screen is visible, and close it when the app goes to the background
While backgrounded, rely on push notifications for milestones such as "Driver has arrived" instead of the live stream
If the socket can't connect (e.g. a proxy blocks it), fall back to polling the trip endpoint every few seconds while the screen is visible
Keep the WebSocket open in a background service for the whole trip so the hidden map is always current
Send the driver's position as an FCM data message every second
questions.explanation: Stream while the user is watching, push for the few events that matter when they're not, and poll only as a fallback. That spends battery and sockets only when they buy something visible. A background socket updating an unseen map wastes battery, and FCM is not a real-time transport: high-frequency messages get throttled, deprioritised or collapsed.

questions.question: Ride-hailing case study: the ETA shown to the rider should be computed on the server from the driver's reported positions, not computed in the rider's app.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The server has live traffic, the routing engine and both parties' data, and it can give the rider, the driver and support the same number. Computing on the client would mean shipping routing data to phones, and each client would show a different ETA. The cost is that ETA updates depend on connectivity, which is acceptable.

questions.question: Instagram-style post: the user picks an 8 MB, 12-megapixel photo, but the feed never displays images wider than 1080px. What should the app do before uploading?
options: Upload the original, since the server can resize it later and keep a full-quality copy
Convert it to PNG so no quality is lost
Base64-encode it and send it inside the JSON post body
Downscale it to about 1080px wide and re-encode it as JPEG/WebP at ~80%
questions.explanation: Spending a little device CPU on resizing cuts the upload to a few hundred KB, which makes it faster, cheaper on cellular data and less likely to fail. The trade-off is losing pixels the product never shows. PNG makes photos much larger, and Base64 adds ~33% overhead and forces the whole image into memory.

questions.question: Media upload case study: the app first asks the API for a pre-signed URL, then PUTs the file straight to object storage. What is the main reason for this design?
options: It lets the app embed the storage account's secret key safely, since the URL hides it
Big uploads bypass the API servers, using a short-lived credential for one object
It removes the need for the user to be authenticated
It means the server never has to validate the uploaded file, since storage checks it
questions.explanation: The API stays in control (it authenticates the user and decides the object key, size and expiry) without carrying the heavy traffic. The cost is an extra round trip to get the URL. Secret keys must never ship in an app, and the server should still validate the object (type, size, scanning) before publishing it.

questions.question: Media upload case study: users post 300 MB videos over flaky mobile networks. Which belong in a robust design? Select all that apply.
options: A chunked, resumable protocol where the client asks the server for the last committed offset and continues from there
Running the upload as WorkManager work with a network constraint, shown as a foreground notification, so it survives app exit and process death
Transcoding on the server into adaptive-bitrate renditions (e.g. HLS) after the upload completes
One big multipart POST that restarts from byte 0 on any failure
Transcoding into every rendition on the device before uploading
questions.explanation: Resumable chunks mean a dropped connection costs at most one chunk, and WorkManager keeps the job alive after the user leaves the app. Server-side transcoding moves the heavy CPU work off the battery. Restarting a 300 MB upload from zero may never finish on a bad network, and encoding many renditions on the phone multiplies both battery use and upload size.

questions.question: Instagram-style post: the media is uploaded, then the app calls `createPost`. The request reaches the server but the response times out, the worker retries, and the user ends up with two identical posts. What is the right fix?
options: Never retry `createPost`, and show an error instead
Before retrying, fetch the user's feed and check whether the post already appears there
Generate a post UUID once on Share and send it as an idempotency key with every attempt
Have the server reject posts with the same caption within 10 seconds
questions.explanation: With an idempotency key, retries are safe because the server stores one key per post and replays the result. The cost is a little server state. Not retrying loses posts on flaky networks, checking the feed races with feed indexing, and deduping on the caption blocks legitimate identical posts. The key is generated once, when the user taps Share, and the server returns the existing post for a repeated key.

questions.question: Instagram-style post: right after the user taps Share, it is reasonable to show the post on their profile using the local image, marked as posting, and to switch it to a failed state with Retry if the upload ultimately fails.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI makes posting feel instant, and the visible pending and failed states keep it honest. The trade-off is extra state to reconcile: the local item is replaced by the server post (matched by client ID) when it succeeds. Hiding the post until a big upload finishes feels broken.

questions.question: Media upload case study: the progress bar shows chunk 7 of 20 and the user taps Cancel. What should the app do?
options: Hide the progress bar but let the upload finish quietly in case the user changes their mind
Cancel the upload work, abort the multipart upload on the server, and drop the pending post
Pause the upload and resume it automatically the next time the app opens, so no bytes are wasted
Delete the source photo from the user's gallery
questions.explanation: Cancel must really stop the work: it saves the user's data, frees the worker, and aborting the multipart upload stops orphaned parts from costing storage (with a lifecycle rule as a backstop if the abort call is lost). Uploading anyway ignores the user's intent, and auto-resuming something they cancelled is a surprise. Cancelling the unique work also cancels the in-flight chunk request.

questions.question: Instagram-style post: the API separates media upload (which returns a `mediaId`) from `createPost(mediaIds, caption)`. Which statements about this split are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The app can start uploading as soon as the photo is picked, while the user is still writing the caption
Media upload can be retried and resumed on its own, while `createPost` stays a small request that is easy to make idempotent
The server can check that each `mediaId` belongs to the user and has finished processing before it publishes the post
It guarantees there are never orphaned uploads in storage
Upload requests no longer need authentication, because `createPost` is authenticated
questions.explanation: Splitting the two hides upload time behind caption writing and keeps the publish step small and safe to retry. The trade-off is the opposite of the tempting option: media that is uploaded but never posted becomes orphaned, so you need a TTL or cleanup job. Each upload must still be authorised, otherwise anyone could fill your storage.

questions.question: Search autocomplete case study: the app sends a request on every keystroke, so typing "kotlin" sends 6 requests. What is the standard first fix?
options: Debounce the input (~300ms) so requests go out only when typing pauses
Search only when the user presses the keyboard's search key, like a normal search form
Send every keystroke over a WebSocket instead of HTTP
Show suggestions only after a 2-second spinner
questions.explanation: Debouncing trades a few hundred milliseconds of latency for far fewer requests, and the suggestions still feel live. Searching only on submit removes autocomplete altogether, and changing the transport doesn't reduce how many queries the backend has to run.

questions.question: Search autocomplete case study: the user types "ko", pauses, then types "kotlin". The slow "ko" response arrives last and overwrites the "kotlin" results. Which operator should replace `???` to prevent this?
options: flatMapConcat
flatMapMerge
flatMapLatest
map
questions.explanation: `flatMapLatest` cancels the inner flow for the previous query as soon as a new query arrives, so an old response can never be shown over a newer one. The cancelled request may be wasted, which is the trade-off. `flatMapMerge` runs the requests in parallel and emits whichever finishes, the exact out-of-order bug, and `flatMapConcat` queues them, adding latency.

questions.question: Search autocomplete case study: since suggestions appear visually under the field, TalkBack users need no extra handling, and they can find the list on their own.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A list that appears without moving focus is silent to a screen reader user. Announce a change (e.g. a polite live region saying "5 suggestions") and make each row a focusable item with a clear label. Use a polite announcement rather than moving focus, because stealing focus while the user is typing is worse.

questions.question: Search autocomplete case study: when the search field is focused and still empty, the app shows the user's recent searches. Where should those come from?
options: A server request made every time the field gains focus, so history syncs across devices
A small, capped, clearable list stored on the device (e.g. DataStore or Room)
An in-memory list that is lost when the process dies
The keyboard's autocorrect dictionary
questions.explanation: A local, capped list shows up instantly, works offline and keeps private history on the device, and the clear option respects privacy. A network call adds latency and fails offline just to show the user's own history, and an in-memory list disappears after process death.

questions.question: Search autocomplete case study: the backend team says suggestion traffic is too high. Which client changes are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Send a query only once it reaches a minimum length (e.g. 2 characters), since one-letter queries are expensive and rarely useful
Keep a small in-memory LRU cache of recent query results keyed by the normalised query, so backspacing and retyping hits the cache
On HTTP 429, pause remote suggestions until `Retry-After` has passed and keep showing local suggestions
Remove the debounce, because `flatMapLatest` already cancels stale requests
Cache every query result forever in an unbounded `HashMap`
questions.explanation: Minimum length, a bounded LRU cache and respecting rate limits each cut server calls with little UX cost. A cached result might be slightly stale, which is fine for suggestions. `flatMapLatest` cancels requests on the client only after they've been sent, so without debounce the server still gets every keystroke, and an unbounded cache is a memory leak.

questions.question: Messaging app search case study: contacts are in a local Room database, and a global user directory is on the server. What should the results list do as the user types, including when the device is offline?
options: Show a spinner until the server responds, then show local and remote results together in one sorted list
Search only the server, since it has a superset of the data
Search only the local database, so results never change while the user is looking at them
Show local matches at once, merge in deduplicated remote results, and keep local ones when offline
questions.explanation: Local-first gives instant results and works offline, and the remote results add coverage when the network is available. The trade-off is a list that grows after a moment, which is handled by deduplicating on a stable ID and appending rather than reshuffling. Waiting on the server makes every search as slow as the network and leaves offline users with nothing. When offline, keep the local results and show a short note that the directory is unavailable.
